newsitem.title: UK: Hewden Stuart up on optimism after H1 data.
newsitem.headline: Hewden Stuart up on optimism after H1 data.

text.p: Shares in British plant hire firm Hewden Stuart Plc gained 4.8 percent on Wednesday after the company released first-half results which dealers said were likely to prompt upwards earnings revisions for the full year.
Hewden Stuart shares traded 6-1/2p higher at 142p by 0725 GMT while the broader market was up 0.3 percent. Some 50,000 shares had changed hands.

"The first-half results were in line with expectations but many feel the company is on course to do better for the full year and there is a lot of talk of shifting earnings forecasts higher," one market maker said.
Hewden Stuart said pretax profit dropped to 14.75 million stg in the first half from 19.73 million a year earlier.
But the group said the decline in the building industry had now levelled off and said trading may improve on the back of the upturn in the housing market and commercial development.
Michael Foster, analyst at Greig Middleton, gave a cautious welcome to the company's statement.

"I am encouraged to be a holder but would defer aggressive buying. We are maintaining our full-year estimate of 31 million stg. That might be nudged up but we want more details on whether prices and utilisation have improved," Foster said.
"I'm not convinced the company has turned around although it certainly isn't getting worse. But it doesn't feel that prices and utilisation are getting better," Foster said.
Foster said his house had been strong buyers in the past of Hewden Stuart on the company's strong cashflow position.

"And by the nature of things, we get a strong profit increase when utilisation rates go in the right direction...if the company meeting (later today) comes out with those details, then I'll be more enthusiastic," he said.
Foster called Hewden Stuart an interesting long term buy but less so for the short-term.

"They committed themselves to too much capital expenditure and have a bias towards civil engeineering and bridges. Therefore cuts in road development will affect them more than others in the industry," Foster warned.
